claim: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) encounters technical challenges in obtaining high-quality nuclei and RNA.
source: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), an alternative to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), encounters technical challenges in obtaining high-quality nuclei and RNA, persistently hindering its applications.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known limitation of the technique.

claim: The presented robust technique for isolating nuclei remarkably enhances snRNA-seq data quality across various tissue types.
source: Here, we present a robust technique for isolating nuclei across various tissue types, remarkably enhancing snRNA-seq data quality.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data quality metrics shown in Figure 2B-F.

claim: The study comprehensively characterizes depot-dependent cellular dynamics of various cell types underlying mouse adipose tissue remodeling during obesity.
source: Employing this approach, we comprehensively characterize the depot-dependent cellular dynamics of various cell types underlying mouse adipose tissue remodeling during obesity.
evidence: This is supported by the snRNA-seq data presented in Figures 2-6 showing different cell populations across depots and conditions.

claim: Distinct adipocyte subpopulations are categorized by size and functionality.
source: By integrating bulk nuclear RNA-seq from adipocyte nuclei of different sizes, we identify distinct adipocyte subpopulations categorized by size and functionality.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4 showing adipocyte subpopulations and their correlation with cell/nucleus size.

claim: Adipocyte subpopulations follow two divergent trajectories: adaptive and pathological.
source: These subpopulations follow two divergent trajectories, adaptive and pathological, with their prevalence varying by depot.
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Dysfunctional hypertrophic adipocytes exhibit a global shutdown in gene expression.
source: Specifically, we identify a key molecular feature of dysfunctional hypertrophic adipocytes, a global shutdown in gene expression, along with elevated stress and inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 6G showing significantly lower UMI and gene counts in Ad6 adipocytes.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing has revolutionized various fields of biology by enabling high-resolution profiling of single-cell heterogeneity within complex tissues.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revolutionized various fields of biology by enabling high-resolution profiling of single-cell heterogeneity within complex tissues (Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2009.

claim: scRNA-seq has facilitated the identification of new cell types and subtypes.
source: It has not only facilitated the identification of new cell types and subtypes (Shaffer et al., 2017), but also uncovered alterations in cellular composition and gene expression across diverse biological contexts during development, disease progression and responses to environmental stimuli (Shalek et al., 2013; Trapnell et al., 2014; Petropoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: scRNA-seq methods require the use of fresh tissues, which can lead to logistic complexities.
source: First, these methods require the use of fresh tissues, which can be difficult to obtain and thus lead to logistic complexities (Alles et al., 2017; Attar et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Lafzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The tissue dissociation process in scRNA-seq can cause cellular stress, leading to reduced cell viability and altered transcriptional profiles.
source: Also, the tissue dissociation process can cause cellular stress, leading to reduced cell viability and altered transcriptional profiles.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation based on general knowledge of the technique.

claim: Adipocytes are incompatible with microfluidic platforms used in the majority of scRNA-seq technologies due to their large size and excess lipid content.
source: Adipocytes are one example; their large size and excess lipid content render them incompatible with the microfluidic platforms used in the majority of scRNA-seq technologies.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation based on the physical properties of adipocytes.

claim: snRNA-seq generates transcriptional profiles with high similarity to those by scRNA-seq.
source: While generating transcriptional profiles with high similarity to those by scRNA-seq (Grindberg et al., 2013; Habib et al., 2017), snRNA-seq offers advantages.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grindberg et al., 2013 and Habib et al., 2017.

claim: snRNA-seq obviates the need for an extended digestion process, minimizing cell type biases and artifactual transcriptional alteration.
source: First, this method utilizes nuclei that are promptly released from tissues during homogenization, obviating the need for an extended digestion process and thereby minimizing cell type biases and artifactual transcriptional alteration.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method based on its mechanism.

claim: snRNA-seq is compatible with cryopreserved samples.
source: Second, its compatibility with cryopreserved samples allows for greater flexibility in experimental designs and enables the utilization of samples stored in biobanks.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: snRNA-seq can be employed to study cell types that are less amenable to scRNA-seq, such as adipocytes and cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, snRNA-seq can be employed to study cell types that are less amenable to scRNA-seq, such as adipocytes and cardiomyocytes, as isolated nuclei no longer retain limiting cellular characteristics and can be loaded on to various platforms.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method based on the properties of isolated nuclei.

claim: Once released from cells, nuclei are highly fragile and susceptible to mechanical stress, resulting in leakage or aggregation.
source: Once released from cells, nuclei are highly fragile and susceptible to mechanical stress, resulting in leakage or aggregation.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge of snRNA-seq.

claim: RNA in isolated nuclei becomes increasingly vulnerable to RNases, leading to rapid RNA degradation.
source: Moreover, their enclosed RNA becomes increasingly vulnerable to RNases, leading to rapid RNA degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge of snRNA-seq.

claim: Adipose tissue plays a pivotal role in energy metabolism, serving as a dynamic energy reservoir within the body.
source: Adipose tissue plays a pivotal role in energy metabolism, serving as a dynamic energy reservoir within the body.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about adipose tissue function.

claim: Adipose tissue exhibits remarkable plasticity in response to nutritional fluctuations.
source: It exhibits remarkable plasticity in response to nutritional fluctuations (Rosen and Spiegelman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosen and Spiegelman, 2014.

claim: In obesity, adipose tissue undergoes a significant remodeling process, expanding substantially to enhance its storage capacity.
source: In obesity, adipose tissue undergoes a significant remodeling process, expanding substantially to enhance its storage capacity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about adipose tissue in obesity.

claim: Adipose tissue remodeling is orchestrated through coordinated actions among diverse cell types, including adipocytes, preadipocytes, endothelial cells, and various immune cells.
source: This process is orchestrated through coordinated actions among diverse cell types, including adipocytes, preadipocytes, endothelial cells, and various immune cells (Corvera, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corvera, 2021.

claim: Prolonged obesity leads to pathological changes and dysfunction in adipose tissue, characterized by disrupted lipid metabolism, impaired insulin signaling, inflammation, and cell death.
source: However, prolonged obesity leads to pathological changes and dysfunction in adipose tissue, characterized by disrupted lipid metabolism, impaired insulin signaling, inflammation, and cell death.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Longo et al., 2019.

claim: Pathological changes in adipose tissue during obesity are critical precursors to the onset of type 2 diabetes and other metabolic diseases.
source: These changes are critical precursors to the onset of type 2 diabetes and other metabolic diseases (Longo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Longo et al., 2019.

claim: The expansion of visceral fat depots increases risks for metabolic disorders, whereas subcutaneous fat depots pose lesser risks or can even offer protection.
source: The expansion of visceral fat depots increases risks for metabolic disorders, whereas subcutaneous fat depots pose lesser risks or can even offer protection (Vishvanath and Gupta, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vishvanath and Gupta, 2019.

claim: Different adipose tissue depots respond differently to obesity.
source: This is likely due to varying responses of different adipose tissue depots to obesity (Pellegrinelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellegrinelli et al., 2016.

claim: In obesity, visceral adipose tissues display enlarged hypertrophic adipocytes, along with hypoxia, elevated fibrosis and inflammation from increased immune cell infiltration.
source: In obesity, visceral adipose tissues display enlarged hypertrophic adipocytes, along with hypoxia, elevated fibrosis and inflammation from increased immune cell infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Longo et al., 2019.

claim: Subcutaneous adipose tissues have smaller adipocytes with lower levels of inflammation and hypoxia compared to visceral adipose tissues in obesity.
source: In contrast, subcutaneous adipose tissues have smaller adipocytes with lower levels of inflammation and hypoxia (Longo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Longo et al., 2019.

claim: scRNA-seq has been used to characterize the dynamics of cell populations underlying adipose tissue remodeling, with a focus on stromal vascular fractions, particularly preadipocytes.
source: scRNA-seq has been used to characterize the dynamics of cell populations underlying adipose tissue remodeling, with a focus on the cell types within stromal vascular fractions, particularly preadipocytes (Schwalie et al., 2018; Burl et al., 2018; Hepler et al., 2018; Merrick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Adipocytes have been excluded from previous scRNA-seq studies of adipose tissue due to technical limitations.
source: Yet adipocytes have been excluded from these studies due to technical limitations.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous studies.

claim: snRNA-seq has revealed evidence of cellular heterogeneity within adipocyte populations.
source: More recently, snRNA-seq has been employed, revealing evidence of the cellular heterogeneity within adipocyte populations (Sárvári et al., 2021; Emont et al., 2022; Holman et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sárvári et al., 2021; Emont et al., 2022; Holman et al., 2023.

claim: Acquiring high-quality snRNA-seq data from adipose tissues remains highly challenging.
source: Despite this progress, acquiring high-quality snRNA-seq data from adipose tissues remains highly challenging.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation in the field.

claim: A wide spectrum of RNA quality was observed among different mouse tissues when no RNase inhibitors were added during nucleus isolation.
source: We observed a wide spectrum of RNA quality among the tissues examined (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The brain exhibited highly intact RNA during nucleus isolation without RNase inhibitors.
source: The brain exhibited highly intact RNA, followed by the heart showing relatively good RNA quality.
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Among adipose tissues, significant RNA degradation was detected, with eWAT showing the highest level of degradation.
source: Among the adipose tissues, including brown adipose tissue, subcutaneous inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT), and visceral epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT), significant RNA degradation was detected, with eWAT showing the highest level of degradation.
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RNA was completely degraded in the pancreas during nucleus isolation without RNase inhibitors.
source: RNA was completely degraded in the pancreas (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The addition of recombinant RNase inhibitors at a concentration of 0.4 U/µl had no discernible effect on RNA quality of any tissues tested.
source: Surprisingly, the addition of recombinant RNase inhibitors at a concentration of 0.4 U/µl had no discernible effect on RNA quality of any of those tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Increasing the concentration of RNase inhibitors to 4 U/µl failed to yield any substantial enhancement in RNA quality.
source: Even when the concentration of RNase inhibitors was increased to 4 U/µl, it failed to yield any substantial enhancement in RNA quality (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental results (data not shown).

claim: The vanadyl ribonucleoside complex (VRC) was identified as having a significant impact on RNA quality during nucleus isolation.
source: Among these, the vanadyl ribonucleoside complex (VRC) (Lienhard et al., 1972) was identified as having a significant impact on RNA quality.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental screening described and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: High-quality RNA with minimal degradation was obtained in all tested tissues except for the pancreas and spleen when using VRC.
source: High-quality RNA with minimal degradation was obtained in all the tested tissues except for the pancreas and its connecting tissue, the spleen (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Combining VRC with recombinant RNase inhibitors yielded further improvements in RNA quality, albeit to a modest extent.
source: Finally, we optimized the protocol by combining VRC with recombinant RNase inhibitors for further improvements, albeit to a modest extent (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The optimized protocol using VRC successfully retrieved a well-dispersed nucleus population without clumps in all tissue types.
source: Using VRC, the optimized protocol successfully retrieved a well-dispersed nucleus population without clumps in all tissue types (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy images shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Nuclei isolated using the optimized protocol showed a smoother membrane surface and larger nucleus size compared to the standard protocol.
source: Further analysis of nucleus morphology at a higher resolution revealed a smoother membrane surface and larger nucleus size when using the optimized protocol, as compared to the standard protocol (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy images shown in Figure 1F.

claim: VRC has preservative function in maintaining tissue morphology.
source: Consistent with the preservative function of VRC proven in maintaining tissue morphology (Shieh et al., 2018), these findings show that our nucleus isolation protocol effectively maintains nucleus structure without shrinkage.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shieh et al., 2018.

claim: Nuclear RNA isolated using the optimized protocol remained intact at 2 and 6 hr post-homogenization, maintaining good quality even after 24 hr.
source: In contrast, nuclear RNA isolated using the optimized protocol remained intact at 2 and 6 hr, maintaining good quality even after 24 hr (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Nuclear RNA from the standard protocol exhibited severe degradation within 2 hr post-homogenization, worsening over 24 hr.
source: In the standard protocol, nuclear RNA exhibited severe degradation within 2 hr post-homogenization, worsening over 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: RNA remained stable in nuclei sorted through flow cytometry, comparable to that of unsorted nuclei.
source: The RNA remained stable, comparable to that of unsorted nuclei (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 1G comparing sorted and unsorted nuclei.

claim: The use of VRC during nucleus isolation does not pose an issue in gene expression profiling.
source: These results indicate that the use of VRC during nucleus isolation does not pose an issue in gene expression profiling.
evidence: This is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 1A.

claim: Strong PCR amplification and highly specific expression of adipocyte markers in adipocyte nuclei and immune/endothelial cell markers in non-adipocyte nuclei were observed using the optimized protocol with VRC.
source: We observed strong PCR amplification and highly specific expression of adipocyte markers in adipocyte nuclei and immune/endothelial cell markers in non-adipocyte nuclei (Figure 2-figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 1A.

claim: The optimized protocol produced high-quality cDNA with long fragment sizes from eWAT and iWAT samples.
source: From eWAT and iWAT samples collected from mice fed either a chow or high fat diet (HFD), we generated high-quality cDNA with long fragment sizes and constructed robust sequencing libraries (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by the bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The datasets from this study displayed significantly higher counts of unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and genes per nucleus compared to other published datasets, exceeding counts by almost twofold.
source: With comparable sequencing depths (Figure 2B), our datasets displayed significantly higher counts of unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and genes per nucleus, exceeding counts from the other datasets by almost twofold (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 2B, C, D.

claim: The proportions of mitochondrial reads in the datasets from this study represented less than 1% (mean 0.37%), which was significantly lower than in other datasets (mean 38.7 and 2.31%).
source: Also, the proportions of mitochondrial reads in our datasets represented less than 1% (mean 0.37%), which was significantly lower than in the other datasets (mean 38.7 and 2.31%; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The optimized method produced substantially higher fractions of reads in nuclei compared to other methods.
source: Importantly, our method produced substantially higher fractions of reads in nuclei (Figure 2F), suggesting low ambient RNA contamination.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The barcode rank plot for the data from this study exhibited a sudden drop of UMI counts, indicating a clear distinction between intact nuclei and background barcodes during cell calling.
source: This was consistent with the barcode rank plot for our data, which exhibited a sudden drop of UMI counts (Figure 2G), indicating a clear distinction between intact nuclei and background barcodes during cell calling.
evidence: This is supported by the barcode rank plots shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CellBender analysis showed a minimal number of cells in the narrow transition zone in the datasets from this study, contrasting with a greater number of cells within the broader transition zone observed in published samples.
source: Analysis using CellBender (Fleming et al., 2023) also contrasted the minimal number of cells in the narrow transition zone in our datasets with the greater number of cells within the broader transition zone observed in the published samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the CellBender analysis shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 1E.

claim: A total of 53,395 cells/nuclei were identified across 10 distinct cell types in the integrated snRNA-seq data from eWAT and iWAT of chow- or HFD-fed mice.
source: After filtering nuclei based on the detected numbers of UMIs and genes, and subsequently removing doublets and ambient RNA, a total of 53,395 cells/nuclei were identified, distributed across 10 distinct cell types (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The major cell types present in adipose tissues included adipocytes, adipocyte progenitor cells (APC), macrophages/monocytes, and endothelial cells.
source: The major cell types present in adipose tissues included adipocytes, adipocyte progenitor cells (APC), macrophages/monocytes, and endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization and proportions shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Less abundant cell types identified included pericytes (PC)/smooth muscle cells (SMC), mesothelial cells, dendritic cells, mast cells, T cells, and B cells.
source: Additionally, we identified less abundant cell types, such as pericytes (PC)/smooth muscle cells (SMC), mesothelial cells, dendritic cells, mast cells, T cells, and B cells.
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization and proportions shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The proportions of cell types in the data from this study largely matched those reported in previous studies, except for the notable improvement in recovering vascular cells.
source: The proportions of these cell types in our data largely matched those reported in previous studies, except for the notable improvement in recovering vascular cells (endothelial cells and PC/SMC) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 2B.

claim: The robust two-step tissue homogenization effectively releases nuclei from vasculature that would otherwise be mechanically resistant.
source: This is likely due to our robust two-step tissue homogenization, which effectively releases nuclei from vasculature that would otherwise be mechanically resistant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the improved recovery of vascular cells.

claim: The UMI and genes per nucleus were higher in every cell type in the data from this study except for adipocytes.
source: We found that the UMI and genes per nucleus were higher in every cell type in our data except for adipocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), which included a dysfunctional subtype with low transcript abundance to be discussed below.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 2D.

claim: HFD resulted in a relative reduction in adipocytes and an increase in macrophage/monocyte fractions in both eWAT and iWAT, with more prominent changes in eWAT.
source: HFD resulted in a relative reduction in adipocytes and an increase in macrophage/monocyte fractions in both eWAT and iWAT, with more prominent changes in eWAT (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2-figure supplement 2E.

claim: APC fractions were smaller in eWAT compared to iWAT under chow diet, with marginal effects under HFD.
source: APC fractions were smaller in eWAT compared to iWAT under chow diet, with marginal effects under HFD.
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2-figure supplement 2E.

claim: The population size of endothelial cells did not show notable differences between the conditions.
source: The population size of endothelial cells did not show notable differences between the conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 2E.

claim: Dendritic cells increased in eWAT in response to HFD.
source: Most of the minor cell populations exhibited minimal differences across the conditions, except for dendritic cells which increased in eWAT in response to HFD, and mast cells which were more abundant in iWAT than eWAT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 2E.

claim: Mast cells were more abundant in iWAT than eWAT.
source: Most of the minor cell populations exhibited minimal differences across the conditions, except for dendritic cells which increased in eWAT in response to HFD, and mast cells which were more abundant in iWAT than eWAT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 2E.

claim: Four different subpopulations of APCs were identified: APC1, APC2, APC3, and APC4.
source: Analysis of APCs revealed four different subpopulations (Figure 3A, B), which generally aligned with prior studies.
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: APC1 and APC2 corresponded to 'adipocyte progenitors', characterized by high expression of both Dpp4 and Pi16.
source: APC1 and APC2 corresponded to 'adipocyte progenitors', characterized by high expression of both Dpp4 and Pi16 (Merrick et al., 2019Merrick et al., 2019), while displaying distinct gene expression profiles from each other (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3-figure supplement 1A, and citation to Merrick et al., 2019.

claim: APC2 exhibited higher expression of fibrotic genes such as Fn1 and Loxl1, resembling 'fibro-inflammatory progenitors'.
source: Notably, APC2 exhibited higher expression of fibrotic genes such as Fn1 and Loxl1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), resembling 'fibro-inflammatory progenitors' (Hepler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 1B and citation to Hepler et al., 2018.

claim: APC3 was identified as 'adipose regulatory cells', expressing F3 (encoding CD142) and showing strong expression of secretory signaling proteins.
source: APC3 was identified as 'adipose regulatory cells', expressing F3 (encoding CD142) and showed strong expression of secretory signaling proteins (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), supporting its paracrine regulatory role (Schwalie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3-figure supplement 1C, and citation to Schwalie et al., 2018.

claim: APC4 represented 'committed preadipocytes', expressing lipid metabolism-related genes such as Lpl, Hsd11b1, and Fabp4.
source: APC4, the largest subpopulation, represented 'committed preadipocytes', expressing lipid metabolism-related genes such as Lpl, Hsd11b1, and Fabp4 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3-figure supplement 1D.

claim: eWAT displayed a higher fraction of APC3 and APC4, while iWAT showed a larger fraction of APC1.
source: The distribution of APC subpopulations differed between adipose depots, with eWAT displaying a higher fraction of APC3 and APC4, while iWAT showed a larger fraction of APC1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In eWAT during obesity, there was an expansion of the APC4 proportion alongside a reduction in APC1 and APC2 populations.
source: Specifically in eWAT, there was an expansion of the APC4 proportion alongside a reduction in APC1 and APC2 populations (Figure 3C) during obesity, suggesting distinct tissue expansion mechanisms in each adipose tissue depot.
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3C.

claim: eWAT appears to promote de novo adipogenesis through conversion of adipocyte progenitors to committed preadipocytes during obesity.
source: eWAT appears to promote de novo adipogenesis through conversion of adipocyte progenitors to committed preadipocytes, as demonstrated in a prior study (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in APC subpopulations and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Seven subpopulations of macrophages and monocytes were identified based on distinct marker expression profiles.
source: We identified seven subpopulations of macrophages and monocytes based on distinct marker expression profiles (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization and marker genes shown in Figure 3D, E and Figure 3-figure supplement 2A.

claim: MC1 and MC2 expressed Clec10a (encoding CD301) and Mrc1 (encoding CD206), indicative of alternatively activated M2 macrophages.
source: The two largest populations, MC1 and MC2, expressed Clec10a (encoding CD301) and Mrc1 (encoding CD206), indicative of alternatively activated M2 macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 2A.

claim: MC2 was enriched for genes associated with antigen presentation and integrin binding, including major histocompatibility complex markers such as H2-Eb1 and H2-Aa.
source: However, MC2 stood out for its enrichment of genes associated with antigen presentation and integrin binding, including major histocompatibility complex markers such as H2-Eb1 and H2-Aa (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis and gene expression shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: MC1 and MC2 cells corresponded to perivascular-like and non-perivascular-like macrophages, respectively, as described by Sárvári et al., 2021.
source: These MC1 and MC2 cells corresponded perivascular-like and non-perivascular-like macrophages, respectively, as described by Sárvári et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sárvári et al., 2021.

claim: MC3 represented 'lipid-associated macrophages (LAMs)', characterized by high expression of lipid metabolism genes.
source: MC3 represented 'lipid-associated macrophages (LAMs)', characterized by high expression of lipid metabolism genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 2D.

claim: MC6 and MC7 resembled previously described regulatory macrophages (RegM) and collagen-expressing macrophages (CEM), respectively.
source: We found two minor macrophage subpopulations, MC6 and MC7, which resembled previously described regulatory macrophages (RegM) and collagen-expressing macrophages (CEM), respectively (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3-figure supplement 2A.

claim: eWAT demonstrated a higher abundance of RegM and iWAT contained more CEM.
source: Their prevalence showed depot-dependent differences, with eWAT demonstrating a higher abundance of RegM and iWAT containing more CEM (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3F.

claim: MC4 and MC5 were identified as classical monocytes and non-classical monocytes, respectively.
source: MC4 and MC5, accounting for approximately 20% of the myelocyte populations, were identified as classical monocytes and non-classical monocytes, respectively (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3-figure supplement 2A.

claim: In response to HFD feeding, only eWAT exhibited a marked relative reduction in MC1 and MC2 populations with a substantial increase in MC3 (LAMs).
source: In response to HFD feeding, only eWAT exhibited a marked relative reduction in MC1 and MC2 populations with a substantial increase in MC3 (LAMs) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Lymphocytes were clustered into four T cell subpopulations – regulatory (Treg), CD4+, CD8+, and natural killer T cells – along with two B cell subpopulations.
source: Lymphocytes were clustered into four T cell subpopulations – regulatory (Treg), CD4+, CD8+, and natural killer T cells – along with two B cell subpopulations (Figure 3G, H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization and marker genes shown in Figure 3G, H and Figure 3-figure supplement 2E.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were more abundant in iWAT, whereas Treg were more prevalent in eWAT.
source: The distribution of T cell subpopulations differed between adipose depots: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were more abundant in iWAT, whereas Treg were more prevalent in eWAT (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3I.

claim: B cells exhibited relatively high homogeneity in proportions between fat depots under chow conditions.
source: Conversely, B cells exhibited relatively high homogeneity in proportions between fat depots under chow conditions (Figure 3G, I).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3G, I.

claim: The most remarkable change in lymphocytes during HFD feeding was the emergence of a small B cell subpopulation, BC2, observed in eWAT.
source: The most remarkable change in lymphocytes during HFD feeding was the emergence of a small B cell subpopulation, BC2, observed in eWAT (Figure 3G), which highly expressed genes involved in B cell proliferation, such as Prkar2b and Mcc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 3G and marker gene expression in Figure 3-figure supplement 2F.

claim: Nine subpopulations of vascular cells were identified, grouped into three major types: blood endothelial cells (blood EC), mural cells, and lymphatic endothelial cells (LEC).
source: We identified nine subpopulations of vascular cells (Figure 3J, K), grouped into three major types: blood endothelial cells (blood EC), mural cells, and lymphatic endothelial cells (LEC) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 3J, K and Figure 3-figure supplement 3A.

claim: Blood EC included venous (VenEC), arterial (ArtEC), and capillary endothelial cells (CapEC).
source: Blood EC included venous (VenEC), arterial (ArtEC), and capillary endothelial cells (CapEC).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3-figure supplement 3B.

claim: CapEC was further divided into arterial capillary endothelial cells (AcapEC) and venous capillary endothelial cells (VcapEC), with the latter being the largest vascular cell type in adipose tissues.
source: CapEC was further divided into arterial capillary endothelial cells (AcapEC) and venous capillary endothelial cells (VcapEC) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), with the latter being the largest vascular cell type in adipose tissues (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 3B and proportions in Figure 3L.

claim: Angiogenic endothelial cells (AngEC) comprise migratory tip cells expressing extracellular matrix (ECM) genes, and proliferative stalk cells with elevated expression of cell cycle genes.
source: We additionally recognized angiogenic endothelial cells (AngEC), comprising migratory tip cells expressing extracellular matrix (ECM) genes, and proliferative stalk cells with elevated expression of cell cycle genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 3B.

claim: An endothelial cell type characterized by high expression of lipid metabolism genes (LipEC) was discovered.
source: Furthermore, we discovered an endothelial cell type characterized by high expression of lipid metabolism genes (LipEC) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the marker gene expression shown in Figure 3-figure supplement 3B.

claim: Following HFD feeding, a relative expansion of AngEC and LipEC was observed in both fat depots.
source: Following HFD feeding, a relative expansion of AngEC and LipEC was observed in both fat depots (Figure 3L), suggesting increased vascularization and lipid transport during obesity-induced adipose tissue expansion.
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3L.

claim: A drastic decrease in the proportion of the VcapEC population was noted specifically within eWAT during HFD feeding.
source: Intriguingly, we noted a drastic decrease in the proportion of the VcapEC population specifically within eWAT during HFD feeding (Figure 3L), indicating impaired metabolite transport into the venous circulation, which may potentially contribute to the pathology of visceral adipose tissue.
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The PC population was notably larger than that of SMC in mural cells.
source: In mural cells, PC and SMC were identified (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), with the PC population notably larger than that of SMC (Figure 3L), consistent with their respective association with capillaries and larger vessels (Rhodin, 1968; Yamazaki and Mukouyama, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3L and citations to Rhodin, 1968 and Yamazaki and Mukouyama, 2018.

claim: LEC comprised 1–3% of the vascular cell population.
source: Lastly, we identified LEC (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), comprising 1–3% of the vascular cell population.
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The fraction of LECs diminished following HFD feeding in both eWAT and iWAT.
source: Interestingly, the fraction of LECs diminished following HFD feeding in both eWAT and iWAT (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The HFD-induced reduction of LEC, along with the decline in VcapEC, implies that metabolic drainage into lymphatic vessels and the venous circulation could be a key pathological feature of visceral adipose tissues during obesity.
source: The HFD-induced reduction of LEC, along with the aforementioned decline in VcapEC, implies that metabolic drainage into lymphatic vessels and the venous circulation could be a key pathological feature of visceral adipose tissues during obesity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in vascular cell populations.

claim: Six subpopulations of adipocytes were identified, characterized by a gradient of unique gene expression signatures among them rather than distinct cell types.
source: In our dataset, we identified six subpopulations of adipocytes, characterized by a gradient of unique gene expression signatures among them rather than distinct cell types (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization and marker genes shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Ad1–Ad3 represented a profile of mature adipocytes with high expression of insulin signaling genes and lipid metabolism genes, with Ad2 demonstrating particularly robust expression of lipid metabolism genes.
source: Ad1–Ad3 represented a profile of mature adipocytes with high expression of insulin signaling genes and lipid metabolism genes, with Ad2 demonstrating particularly robust expression of lipid metabolism genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4-figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ad3, along with Ad4, showed elevated expression of genes associated with cell junction, ECM organization and calcium homeostasis.
source: Ad3, along with Ad4, also showed elevated expression of genes associated with cell junction, ECM organization and calcium homeostasis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4-figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ad6 was distinguished by its pronounced expression of genes involved in unfolded protein binding, oxidative stress, cytoskeleton, antigen presentation, and adipokines such as Lep, Retn, and Rbp4.
source: Ad6 was distinguished by its pronounced expression of genes involved in unfolded protein binding, oxidative stress, cytoskeleton, antigen presentation, and adipokines such as Lep, Retn, and Rbp4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4-figure supplement 1C.

claim: In response to HFD feeding, the proportions of Ad1 and Ad2 were significantly reduced in both eWAT and iWAT, while Ad3 showed a relative increase in iWAT.
source: In response to HFD feeding, the proportions of Ad1 and Ad2 were significantly reduced in both eWAT and iWAT, while Ad3 showed a relative increase in iWAT.
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4-figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Ad6 proportion exhibited a substantial increase in eWAT and a moderate rise in iWAT in response to HFD feeding.
source: Notably, the Ad6 proportion exhibited a substantial increase in eWAT and a moderate rise in iWAT (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4-figure supplement 1D.

claim: Enlarged nuclei were observed in hypertrophic adipocytes isolated from HFD-fed mice.
source: Interestingly, we observed enlarged nuclei in hypertrophic adipocytes isolated from HFD-fed mice (Figure 4D), which correlated positively with adipocyte cell size in both fat depots (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy images shown in Figure 4D and correlation analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: There is a positive correlation between nuclear GFP intensity and adipocyte nucleus size in NuTRAP mice.
source: Profiling adipocyte nuclei labeled with GFP and mCherry from NuTRAP mice fed on chow or HFD showed a strong positive correlation between nuclear GFP intensity and adipocyte nucleus size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4-figure supplement 1E.

claim: eWAT and iWAT from chow-fed mice primarily displayed smaller adipocyte nuclei.
source: eWAT and iWAT from chow-fed mice primarily displayed smaller adipocyte nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F, G.

claim: In HFD-fed mice, eWAT predominantly contained larger adipocyte nuclei, while iWAT showed a heterogeneous size range from small to large nuclei.
source: In HFD-fed mice, eWAT predominantly contained larger adipocyte nuclei, while iWAT showed a heterogeneous size range from small to large nuclei (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F, G.

claim: Large adipocytes promote processes involved in insulin response, vascularization and DNA repair, while inhibiting processes related to cell migration, metabolism and the cytoskeleton.
source: Differential gene expression analysis followed by gene ontology analysis revealed that large adipocytes promote processes involved in insulin response, vascularization and DNA repair, while inhibiting processes related to cell migration, metabolism and the cytoskeleton (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is supported by the differential gene expression and GO analysis shown in Figure 4-figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Adipocyte hypertrophy signature genes exhibited higher overall expression levels in adipocyte nuclei in iWAT from HFD-fed mice compared to those from chow-fed mice.
source: They also exhibited higher overall expression levels in adipocyte nuclei in iWAT from HFD-fed mice compared to those from chow-fed mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 4H.

claim: High expression of hypertrophy signature genes was observed in Ad3–Ad4 and Ad5–Ad6 adipocyte subpopulations.
source: When overlaying the expression of these hypertrophy signature genes across adipocyte subpopulations, we observed high expression in Ad3–Ad4 and Ad5–Ad6 (Figure 4I), suggesting that they may represent hypertrophic adipocytes.
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Ad3 represents 'metabolically healthy hypertrophic (MHH)' adipocytes, while Ad6 represents 'metabolically unhealthy hypertrophic (MUH)' adipocytes.
source: This implies that Ad3 represents 'metabolically healthy hypertrophic (MHH)' adipocytes, while Ad6 represents 'metabolically unhealthy hypertrophic (MUH)' adipocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distinct expression patterns of insulin signaling and lipid metabolism genes between Ad3 and Ad6.

claim: Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed two divergent trajectories: one toward Ad3 and Ad4 depicting an 'adaptive healthy transition', and another toward Ad5 and Ad6 indicating a 'maladaptive dysfunctional transition'.
source: To further discern the obesity-driven dynamics of adipocyte subpopulations, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis, starting with the Ad1–Ad2 subpopulations that were prevalent under chow conditions (Figure 4J). Two divergent trajectories were revealed: One trajectory moves toward Ad3 and Ad4, which may depict an 'adaptive healthy transition'. Conversely, the alternate trajectory progresses toward Ad5 and ultimately to Ad6, indicating a potential 'maladaptive dysfunctional transition'.
evidence: This is supported by the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The dysfunctional trajectory leading to Ad6 was dominant in eWAT while the adaptive trajectory toward Ad3 remained more prevalent in iWAT during HFD feeding.
source: Importantly, eWAT and iWAT displayed contrasting preferences in adipocyte trajectories during HFD feeding: the dysfunctional trajectory leading to Ad6 was dominant in eWAT while the adaptive trajectory toward Ad3 remained more prevalent in iWAT (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Gene cluster 1 represented genes generally upregulated by HFD across all adipocyte subpopulations, with the most significant induction observed in Ad3.
source: Gene cluster 1 represented a group of genes generally upregulated by HFD across all subpopulations, with the most significant induction observed in Ad3, followed by Ad4 and Ad2 to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Genes in cluster 1 associated with cell junctions, ECM and the cytoskeleton describe biological responses during HFD-induced adipose tissue remodeling.
source: The genes associated with cell junctions, ECM and the cytoskeleton included in this cluster (Figure 5B) may describe biological responses during HFD-induced adipose tissue remodeling, which were featured in the aforementioned adaptive transition, among Ad2-Ad4 subpopulations.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Gene clusters 2 and 3 comprised genes up- and down-regulated, respectively, with changes most pronounced in Ad6 and to a lesser extent in Ad5, during HFD feeding.
source: On the other hand, Gene clusters 2 and 3 comprised genes up- and down-regulated, respectively, with changes most pronounced in Ad6 and to a lesser extent in Ad5, during HFD feeding.
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The induction of genes in cluster 2 and repression of genes in cluster 3 reflect stress response, inflammation, and cell death in adipose tissues, along with impaired machinery regulating gene expression during HFD-induced adipose pathology.
source: The induction of genes in cluster 2, as well as the repression of genes in cluster 3, reflect stress response, inflammation, and cell death in adipose tissues, along with impaired machinery regulating gene expression (e.g., chromatin remodeling and mRNA metabolic process) during HFD-induced adipose pathology (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genes in cluster 4, commonly down-regulated by HFD across all adipocyte subpopulations, had enriched metabolic processes such as lipid metabolism, thermogenesis, and insulin phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) signaling.
source: Genes in cluster 4, commonly down-regulated by HFD across all adipocyte subpopulations, had enriched metabolic processes such as lipid metabolism, thermogenesis, and insulin phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) signaling (Figure 5B), indicating a general decline in metabolic activity and insulin sensitivity across the entire adipocyte population rather than specific subpopulations.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Markedly higher H2DCFDA fluorescence intensity was observed in eWAT and a modest increase in iWAT under HFD conditions, resulting in a significantly larger fraction of H2DCFDA-positive adipocytes, especially in eWAT.
source: Under HFD conditions, we observed markedly higher H2DCFDA fluorescence intensity in eWAT and a modest increase in iWAT, resulting in a significantly larger fraction of H2DCFDA-positive adipocytes, especially in eWAT (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: B2M was strongly detected in eWAT and slightly in iWAT after HFD feeding, particularly within crown-like structures (CLS) and in the cytoplasm of adipocytes neighboring these CLS.
source: B2M was strongly detected in eWAT and slightly in iWAT after HFD feeding. B2M was particularly found within crown-like structures (CLS), as well as in the cytoplasm of adipocytes neighboring these CLS (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is supported by the whole-mount immunostaining images and quantification shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: Dead adipocytes are detected within crown-like structures (CLS).
source: As dead adipocytes are detected within CLS (Murano et al., 2008), this result suggests Ad6 as stressed and dying cells due to inflammation, both within and outside the CLS.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Murano et al., 2008.

claim: A significant proportion of adipocyte nuclei from eWAT in HFD-fed mice lacked PPARγ proteins.
source: While most GFP-labeled adipocyte nuclei robustly expressed PPARγ proteins under typical conditions, a significant proportion of adipocyte nuclei from eWAT in HFD-fed mice lacked PPARγ proteins (Figure 6E, F), confirming the presence of PPARγ-deficient Ad6 adipocytes in eWAT during obesity.
evidence: This is supported by the whole-mount immunostaining images and quantification shown in Figure 6E, F.

claim: Ad6 does not represent dedifferentiating adipocytes.
source: We did not detect significant expression of APC markers such as Pdgfra in Ad6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), indicating that Ad6 does not represent dedifferentiating adipocytes.
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 4-figure supplement 1I.

claim: Ad6 adipocytes undergo a global loss of gene expression, as indicated by substantially fewer transcripts detected.
source: Instead, the substantially fewer transcripts, represented by UMIs or genes, detected in the Ad6 subpopulation (Figure 6G), suggests Ad6 adipocytes undergo a global loss of gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by the violin plots shown in Figure 6G.

claim: A comparable adipocyte population to Ad6 was identified in the previous study by Emont et al., 2022 (mAd3).
source: In the integration of our data with previous datasets, we observed a comparable adipocyte population identified in the previous study (mAd3 in Emont et al., 2022Emont et al., 2022; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), with similar marker gene expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and lower transcript abundance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the integration analysis shown in Figure 6-figure supplement 1A, B, C.

claim: The population size of mAd3 was much smaller than Ad6 in the data from this study and did not show consistent population changes during obesity.
source: However, the population size of mAd3 was much smaller than Ad6 in our data and did not show consistent population changes during obesity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the proportions shown in Figure 6-figure supplement 1D.

claim: The discrepancy in detecting the Ad6/mAd3 population may be due to different technical robustness between protocols.
source: This discrepancy may be due to different technical robustness; the dysfunctional cellular state of this population, with severely compromised RNA contents, may have made it difficult to accurately capture using standard protocols in the previous study, while our protocol enabled robust and precise detection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in data quality and population detection.

claim: Brain tissue exhibited the lowest RNase activity among the tissues examined.
source: Notably, brain tissue, which has been primarily used in prior snRNA-seq studies, exhibited the lowest RNase activity.
evidence: This is based on the RNA quality data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Standard nucleus isolation protocols employed in brain studies may not readily translate to other tissues, particularly those with high RNase activities.
source: This implies that the standard nucleus isolation protocols employed in those studies may not readily translate to other tissues, particularly those with high RNase activities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variation in RNA quality across tissues.

claim: Recombinant RNase inhibitor proteins specifically target certain RNase types, such as RNase A, 1, and T1.
source: However, these inhibitors marginally improved RNA quality, likely due to their specific targeting of certain RNase types, such as RNase A, 1, and T1.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the limited effectiveness of recombinant RNase inhibitors.

claim: VRC functions as a transition state analog, binding to the active sites of RNases and inhibiting their enzymatic activity.
source: VRC functions as a transition state analog, binding to the active sites of RNases and inhibiting their enzymatic activity (Gray, 1974; Berger and Birkenmeier, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gray, 1974 and Berger and Birkenmeier, 1979.

claim: The application of VRC in gene expression studies has been limited due to its inhibitory effects on other RNA enzymes, including reverse transcriptase.
source: Despite its demonstrated versatility in RNA experiments (Gray, 1974; Berger and Birkenmeier, 1979; Egberts et al., 1977), the application of VRC in gene expression studies has been limited due to its inhibitory effects on other RNA enzymes, including reverse transcriptase (Berger and Birkenmeier, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The method addressed the issue of VRC inhibiting reverse transcriptase by reducing VRC from nucleus isolation buffer prior to loading onto microfluidic devices.
source: Our method addressed this issue by reducing VRC from nucleus isolation buffer prior to loading onto microfluidic devices, as confirmed by the robust qRT-PCR and snRNA-seq results we obtained.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological solution and confirmed by experimental results.

claim: A few protocols have been introduced to enhance RNA quality by employing VRC or acidic buffers during nucleus isolation for snRNA-seq, particularly for kidney and pancreas samples.
source: Recently, we encountered a few protocols that have been introduced to enhance RNA quality by employing VRC or acidic buffers during nucleus isolation for snRNA-seq, particularly for kidney (Soccio et al., 2014) and pancreas (Tosti et al., 2021) samples.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soccio et al., 2014 and Tosti et al., 2021.

claim: The applicability of previous VRC-based protocols to other tissue types remains untested.
source: However, their applicability to other tissue types remains untested.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous protocols.

claim: The optimized protocol successfully preserved both nuclear RNA quality and the integrity of the nuclear structure in various tissue types.
source: In contrast, our optimized protocol successfully preserved not only nuclear RNA quality in various tissue types, but also the integrity of the nuclear structure.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1C-F.

claim: VRC has preservative properties, protecting tissue morphology, as well as RNA, protein, and genomic DNA quality.
source: This observation aligns with a recent study that demonstrated the preservative properties of VRC, protecting tissue morphology, as well as RNA, protein, and genomic DNA quality (Shieh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shieh et al., 2018.

claim: The optimized protocol offers greater flexibility for snRNA-seq experiments, allowing nucleus isolation and loading onto microfluidic devices to be performed on different days if necessary.
source: Considering that snRNA-seq experiments typically require completion of nucleus isolation and loading onto microfluidic devices (e.g., 10x Genomics Chromium controller) within a narrow time window on the same day, our protocol offers greater flexibility for these critical steps, allowing them to be performed on different days if necessary.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage based on the temporal stability data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The optimized protocol will enable patient biopsies to be collected for diagnostic tests and then analyzed via snRNA-seq at a different facility in the clinical setting.
source: In the clinical setting, for example, this will enable patient biopsies to be collected for diagnostic tests and then be analyzed via snRNA-seq at a different facility.
evidence: This is a speculative application based on the temporal stability of the protocol.

claim: The single-nucleus atlas of mouse white adipose tissues generally aligns with previous studies while offering deeper insights into depot specificity and cellular composition dynamics during obesity.
source: Our single-nucleus atlas of mouse white adipose tissues generally aligns with previous studies while offering deeper insights into depot specificity and cellular composition dynamics during obesity.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the comprehensive data presented in Figures 2-6.

claim: The marked decrease in the proportion of capillary endothelial cells in eWAT during HFD feeding is consistent with previously documented capillary rarefaction and elevated hypoxia associated with adipose tissue expansion.
source: We observed a marked decrease in the proportion of capillary endothelial cells in eWAT specifically during HFD feeding, consistent with the previously documented capillary rarefaction and elevated hypoxia associated with adipose tissue expansion (Rosen and Spiegelman, 2014; Pasarica et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3L and citations to Rosen and Spiegelman, 2014 and Pasarica et al., 2009.

claim: Defective drainage of metabolites and molecules into the venous circulation may be a key feature of dysfunctional adipose tissue in obesity.
source: These findings suggest that defective drainage of metabolites and molecules into the venous circulation may be another key feature of dysfunctional adipose tissue in obesity, warranting further investigation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in VcapEC and LEC populations.

claim: Adipocyte cell size is a key determinant of adipocyte clustering in mice.
source: Therefore, by isolating adipocyte nuclei of various sizes from iWAT, we identified gene signatures that determine adipocyte hypertrophy. Overlaying this data with snRNA-seq data revealed that cell size is a key determinant of adipocyte clustering in mice.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between nucleus size and adipocyte subpopulations shown in Figures 4D-I.

claim: In human adipocytes, insulin sensitivity is shown to be a primary factor in adipocyte classification rather than cell size.
source: This finding contrasts with the heterogeneity of human adipocytes, where insulin sensitivity is shown to be a primary factor in adipocyte classification rather than cell size, as demonstrated by spatial transcriptomics mapping (Massier et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Massier et al., 2023.

claim: Ex vivo differentiated human adipocytes derived from various donors displayed distinct cellular phenotypes, consistent with the heterogeneity in adipocyte subpopulations identified by snRNA-seq.
source: Interestingly, ex vivo differentiated human adipocytes derived from various donors displayed distinct cellular phenotypes, consistent with the heterogeneity in adipocyte subpopulations identified by snRNA-seq (Emont et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Emont et al., 2022.

claim: Significant genetic variation among humans potentially serves as a major driver of adipocyte clustering, overriding the size-dependent differences found in inbred mouse strains.
source: This suggests that the significant genetic variation among humans, potentially serving as a major driver of adipocyte clustering, overrides the size-dependent differences found in inbred mouse strains with homogeneous genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between human and mouse adipocyte heterogeneity.

claim: Small white adipocytes from Rhesus Macaques monkeys exhibit mosaic lipid transport activity.
source: For instance, despite both Ad1 and Ad2 subpopulations having small cell size and abundance under chow conditions, they exhibited distinct expression levels of lipid metabolism genes. This finding may be consistent with previous studies demonstrating mosaic lipid transport activity among small white adipocytes from Rhesus Macaques monkeys (Varlamov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varlamov et al., 2015.

claim: Calcium deposits are frequently observed in obese adipocytes.
source: Also, the unique enrichment of genes involved in calcium transport and ossification in hypertrophic Ad4 adipocytes may account for the frequent occurrence of calcium deposits observed in obese adipocytes (Giordano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Giordano et al., 2013.

claim: MUH adipocytes are primarily found around crown-like structures in obese eWAT with oxidative stress and inflammation markers.
source: We not only validated the presence of MUH adipocytes, primarily around CLS in obese eWAT with oxidative stress and inflammation markers, but also discovered their potential association with prolonged obesity through pseudotime analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 6A-D and the pseudotime analysis in Figure 4J.

claim: MUH adipocytes showed deficient expression of the master transcriptional regulator PPARγ as well as a substantial decline in metabolic gene expression.
source: Interestingly, MUH adipocytes showed deficient expression of the master transcriptional regulator PPARγ as well as a substantial decline in metabolic gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 6E, F and Figure 4-figure supplement 1A.

claim: Adipocytes fail to maintain their identity during obesity.
source: This aligns with our earlier findings, which demonstrated the failure of adipocytes to maintain their identity during obesity (Roh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roh et al., 2020.

claim: Ad6 adipocytes are comparable to 'stressed lipid-scavenging' adipocytes described by Sárvári et al., 2021.
source: The significant decrease in transcript counts in Ad6 suggests that these cells may represent stressed or dying cells, akin to the 'stressed lipid-scavenging' adipocytes described by Sárvári et al., 2021.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of Ad6 and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Human adipocyte heterogeneity does not correspond well to that of mouse adipocytes.
source: Notably, human adipocyte heterogeneity does not correspond well to that of mouse adipocytes (Massier et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Massier et al., 2023.

claim: Human adipocyte data show poor reproducibility between different studies.
source: Furthermore, human adipocyte data show poor reproducibility between different studies (Massier et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Massier et al., 2023.

claim: The inconsistency in adipocyte heterogeneity is unique to adipocytes, as other cell types in adipose tissues display consistent sub cell types across species and studies.
source: Interestingly, this inconsistency is unique to adipocytes, as other cell types in adipose tissues display consistent sub cell types across species and studies (Massier et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Massier et al., 2023.

claim: Adipocytes may exhibit a unique pathological cellular state with significantly reduced RNA content, which may contribute to poor consistency in adipocyte heterogeneity in prior studies with suboptimal RNA quality.
source: Our findings indicate that adipocytes may exhibit a unique pathological cellular state with significantly reduced RNA content, which may contribute to the poor consistency in adipocyte heterogeneity in prior studies with suboptimal RNA quality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed characteristics of Ad6 and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Using a robust method to effectively preserve RNA quality may be critical for accurately characterizing adipocyte populations, especially in disease states.
source: Therefore, using a robust method to effectively preserve RNA quality may be critical for accurately characterizing adipocyte populations, especially in disease states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the improved detection of Ad6 using the optimized protocol.

claim: Ad2–Ad4 adipocytes undergo tissue remodeling for enhanced adipose functionality, such as storage capacity.
source: For instance, Ad2–Ad4 adipocytes appeared to undergo tissue remodeling for enhanced adipose functionality, such as storage capacity.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Traditional features of dysfunctional adipose tissue, including inflammation, cell death, and stress response, were predominantly derived from Ad5–Ad6 adipocytes.
source: In contrast, the traditional features of dysfunctional adipose tissue, including inflammation, cell death, and stress response, were predominantly derived from Ad5–Ad6 adipocytes.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ad5–Ad6 adipocytes were responsible for chromatin alterations and defective gene expression.
source: They were also responsible for chromatin alterations and defective gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The core functions of adipocytes, including lipid metabolism and insulin signaling, were generally impaired in all adipocyte subpopulations during obesity.
source: On the other hand, the core functions of adipocytes, including lipid metabolism and insulin signaling, were generally impaired in all adipocyte subpopulations.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PPARγ agonists, such as thiazolidinediones, are outstandingly effective in improving adipose function and glucose homeostasis, surpassing the effects of other anti-inflammatory or anti-stress reagents.
source: The distinctions between obesity-induced features occurring in the entire adipocyte population versus specific adipocyte subpopulations may explain the outstanding effectiveness of PPARγ agonists, such as thiazolidinediones, in improving adipose function and glucose homeostasis (Soccio et al., 2014), surpassing the effects of other anti-inflammatory or anti-stress reagents (Kraakman et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; da Cruz Nascimento et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differential contributions of adipocyte subpopulations and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Therapeutic approaches need to be tailored based on the specific biological processes to be targeted to improve adipose tissue function during obesity.
source: Our discovery emphasizes the need to tailor therapeutic approaches based on the specific biological processes to be targeted to improve adipose tissue function during obesity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential contributions of adipocyte subpopulations to various pathways.
